title: Error Handling: Exceptions vs. Return Codes
description: How Python's and Java's exception-based error handling compares to C's return-code convention.
objectives: Understand the tradeoffs between the two approaches

content.heading: Python
content.body: Errors are represented as exceptions, raised with raise and handled with try/except/else/finally. Nearly every kind of failure (bad input, missing file, division by zero) surfaces as an exception, which propagates up the call stack automatically until caught — there's no need to manually check a return value for 'did this fail' after every single call.

content.heading: Java
content.body: Errors are also represented as exceptions (try/catch/finally, throw, throws), with a key structural distinction Python and C both lack: checked exceptions, which the compiler forces you to either catch or explicitly declare a method might propagate — a deliberate design choice to make certain failure modes (like file I/O) impossible to silently ignore at compile time.

content.heading: C
content.body: C has no exception mechanism at all. The near-universal convention is returning a special value (often -1, NULL, or a nonzero integer) to signal failure, which the caller must remember to explicitly check after every call — nothing in the language enforces this, and forgetting to check a return value is a common, entirely silent source of bugs. Some failure conditions instead manifest as direct undefined behavior (like NULL pointer dereference) rather than any kind of signaled error at all.

content.heading: Key Differences
content.body: Python's and Java's exceptions propagate automatically and can't be silently ignored (an uncaught exception crashes the program loudly, with a traceback, rather than silently continuing with bad data) — Java additionally enforces at compile time that certain exceptions be acknowledged. C's return-code convention requires the programmer's active discipline at every single call site, with the compiler providing zero enforcement, and ignoring a failure typically continues execution with invalid/garbage data rather than stopping loudly.

content.heading: When It Matters
content.body: The consequence of forgetting to handle a possible failure differs sharply: in Python/Java, an unhandled exception is loud and immediate (the program stops with a clear error); in C, an unchecked return code typically results in silent, delayed misbehavior, often far from the actual point of failure — a significant reason C code demands more careful, disciplined error-checking habits.

keyPoints: Python and Java both use exceptions that propagate automatically and can't be silently ignored
Java uniquely enforces checked exceptions at compile time for certain failure categories
C has no exceptions — failure is signaled via return codes, which the programmer must remember to check manually, with no compiler enforcement
